analysis.one_liner: Bans new fossil fuel power plants, fracking everywhere, and exports of US crude oil and natural gas.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in three House committees when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to make it illegal for any new fossil fuel power plant to emit greenhouse gases, ban hydraulic fracturing on all US onshore and offshore land starting January 1, 2025, and prohibit exports of domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, including LNG. It also bars federal approval of new LNG terminals unless they demonstrably reduce emissions. Its stated goal is transitioning the country off fossil fuels to protect against climate change.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans facing climate impacts, communities living near fracking operations and fossil fuel infrastructure, and future generations. The bill's findings specifically emphasize frontline environmental justice communities and a just transition for fossil fuel workers, including union training for clean-energy jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any greenhouse gas emission from new fossil fuel power plants starting immediately upon enactment, preventing new fossil generation.
Bans hydraulic fracturing on all US onshore and offshore land, effective January 1, 2025, eliminating a major source of methane pollution and groundwater contamination.
Prohibits exports of domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, including LNG, keeping domestic energy supply at home.
Bars FERC from approving new LNG terminal applications or issuing certificates unless they demonstrably reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers who rely on fracking, LNG terminal operators and developers, fossil fuel exporters, and coal/gas power companies building new plants. Fossil fuel workers in affected sectors would face job disruption, though the bill's findings call for a just transition with union training.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

drawbacks.text: Banning fracking and exports simultaneously would sharply reduce domestic oil and gas production and could raise energy prices in the short term, at a time when the bill's own findings note the need for a transition rather than an abrupt cutoff.

The bill has no worker compensation or transition funding mechanism in its text; it states Congress's intent for a just transition in findings but provides no appropriations or program for displaced fossil fuel workers.
The emissions ban applies to new units only, leaving existing fossil fuel power plants and infrastructure untouched, so it does not by itself achieve the emissions reductions its findings call for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A serious climate bill with genuine public health and long-term climate benefits for ordinary people, but its abrupt production and export bans would impose real short-term costs on energy consumers and fossil fuel workers, and its transition language is aspirational rather than funded. The scope is broad and the bill was drafted as a statement of priorities rather than a carefully staged phaseout.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in December 2021 and referred to three House committees, but it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 7, 2021, with 22 original cosponsors and referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change on December 8 and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on December 17, 2021, and received no further action.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, LNG terminal developers, and fossil fuel exporters benefit from the bill's failure, since fracking, new fossil generation, and crude oil and natural gas exports all continue unrestricted. House leadership and committee chairs who never scheduled it for action also face no political cost for the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

for.name: 22 original House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; total cosponsors grew to 26, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Would have lost fracking operations, LNG terminal approvals, and export markets if the bill had passed; the industry broadly opposed fracking bans and export restrictions during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans supported the bill, and it never reached a floor vote where partisan divisions could be measured.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill bans fracking on all US land starting January 1, 2025, eliminating their core extraction method. Fracking operations generate local pollution and water contamination costs borne by nearby communities.

industries.industry: LNG terminal developers and natural gas exporters
industries.note: The bill bars new LNG terminal approvals and prohibits natural gas exports, cutting off major expansion revenue. Export-driven LNG demand raises domestic natural gas prices paid by US consumers.
The bill reinstates a ban on crude oil exports, reversing the 2015 lifting of the ban and restricting producers to domestic markets.

industries.industry: New fossil fuel power plant developers
industries.note: The bill prohibits any greenhouse gas emissions from new electric utility steam generating units, effectively barring new coal and gas plants.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean technology firms
industries.note: Blocking new fossil generation and fracking accelerates demand for wind, solar, storage, and grid infrastructure, expanding markets for clean energy suppliers.
